paper.title: Multi messenger study of GRB 221009A with VHE gamma-ray and neutrino Afterglow from a Gaussian structured jet
paper.abstract: Recent detections of very-high-energy (VHE; ≳ 100 GeV) emission from GRB afterglows, most notably the unprecedented brightness of GRB 221009A observed by LHAASO, reveal emission components beyond the standard electron synchrotron model. The multi-TeV photons motivate synchrotron self-Compton and possibly hadronic contributions, while the non-detection of coincident neutrinos by IceCube/KM3NeT/GRAND200k constrains the microphysical parameters, jet kinetic energy and ambient medium density. We model the VHE afterglow of GRB 221009A with an external forward shock from a Gaussian structured jet in a uniform density medium. This angular structure reproduces the extreme TeV output at an off-axis angle but without demanding large energies as in a top-hat jet. We also compute the corresponding pγ neutrino flux in the PeV-EeV energies and derive a time-integrated upper limit based on the effective area of IceCube Gen2 and GRAND200k. This provides us with insights into the contributions of individual GRBs to the neutrino events. The predicted neutrino flux for GRB 221009A with model parameters inferred from multi-wavelength spectral energy distribution lies below the sensitivities of these detectors. Even our correlation analysis, optimized to search for neutrino signals by the upcoming GRAND200k, infers that the events from this GRB are of order ~ 0.1 under a highly optimistic microphysical parameter regime. We also compare the variation in neutrino flux arising from on-axis and off-axis jet viewing geometries, and conclude that it can account for approximately an order of magnitude difference in the neutrino signal. Thus, our studies conclude that a brighter burst occurring closer than GRB 221009A would be crucial for any neutrino detections by upcoming neutrino telescopes. Future GRB detections by the Cherenkov Telescope Array will provide important constraints on their geometry, radiation mechanisms, and any potential associated neutrino signals.

paper.title: NICER view of energy-dependent eclipse signatures and structured stellar wind in 4U 1538-522
paper.abstract: 4U 1538--522 is a persistent, wind-fed, eclipsing, high mass X-ray binary. In this work, its eclipse timing analysis with NICER has been performed using August 2021 observations. The data covered complete X-ray eclipse of the neutron star, including ingress and egress transitions. The spin period of the neutron star was 526.403(1) s at MJD 59431 with mid-eclipse ephemeris at MJD 59431.816(16). The hardness ratio evolved during these observations from an average value of 0.48 to 1.07, with the source hardest during eclipse ingress and egress. The pulse profiles showed strong dependence on hardness as well as energy, indicating changes in the emission and absorption geometry across the orbital phase. The energy dependent eclipse duration and asymmetric ingress/egress timescales provide direct evidence for a structured and inhomogeneous stellar wind. The inferred smearing timescale indicates an extended scattering region of size ~ 10<SUP>11</SUP> cm associated with enhanced density, consistent with an accretion wake trailing the neutron star. In addition, flickering ingress/egress suggests the presence of small clumpy structures in the stellar wind, with effects more pronounced at lower energies due to stronger absorption. paper.title: On the apparent correlation between X-ray and neutrino luminosities of active galactic nuclei
paper.abstract: Recent studies have reported a linear correlation between the hard X-ray and high-energy neutrino luminosities of active galactic nuclei (AGN), suggesting a possible physical connection between these two messengers. In this work, we challenge this interpretation by demonstrating that the observed correlation may arise purely from selection effects. We analyze 10 years of IceCube public data for a sample of Seyfert galaxies and blazars from the Swift BAT catalog. While our data reproduces the apparent L<SUB>ν</SUB>--L<SUB>X</SUB> correlation for sources with mild (but not significant) neutrino evidence, we show through Monte Carlo simulations that the same correlation appears even when analyzing random sky positions with no astrophysical sources. The key issue is that TS-based source selection effectively restricts the neutrino flux to a narrow range (a factor of several), while the luminosity distance of the sample spans ~ 4 orders of magnitude. This causes the luminosity <mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mi>L</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>4</mml:mn><mml:mi>π</mml:mi><mml:msubsup><mml:mi>D</mml:mi><mml:mi>L</mml:mi><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:msubsup><mml:mi>F</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:math> to be dominated by the distance term rather than intrinsic flux variations, creating an artificial correlation. While a robust flux correlation (F<SUB>ν</SUB>--F<SUB>X</SUB>) for high-significance sources may indicate a genuine physical link, our results demonstrate that a luminosity-luminosity correlation alone is insufficient to establish a physical relationship between neutrino and X-ray emission in AGN.

paper.title: Revisiting the 2021 outburst of the BHC MAXI J1803-298 using NICER, NuSTAR, and Insight-HXMT data
paper.abstract: We present a broadband spectral and timing study of the black hole candidate MAXI J1803--298 during its 2021 outburst using simultaneous observations from NICER, NuSTAR, and Insight-HXMT. The combined multi-instrument coverage allows us to investigate the evolution of low-frequency quasi-periodic oscillations (LFQPOs) together with the spectral properties of the source over a wide energy range. During the early observation epoch, the source exhibits a hard or hard-intermediate spectral state dominated by Comptonized emission with reflection features. Spectral modeling within the framework of the two-component advective flow (TCAF) model indicates the presence of a sub-Keplerian halo and a Keplerian disk with a shock located at ~ 130 Schwarzschild radii, and provides an independent estimate of the black hole mass. A prominent LFQPO is detected during this epoch with a centroid frequency evolving from ~ 0.35 Hz to ~ 0.5 Hz and extending up to ~ 100 keV. The energy-dependent fractional rms variability suggests that the modulation originates primarily from the Comptonizing inner accretion flow. In contrast, a later observation epoch shows a softer spectral state characterized by stronger disk emission and a steeper photon index, during which no LFQPO is detected. We also demonstrate that cospectral analysis effectively mitigates dead-time-induced distortions in NuSTAR timing studies, confirming the intrinsic nature of the detected variability. The combined spectral and timing results support a scenario in which LFQPOs in MAXI J1803--298 arise from the dynamically evolving inner accretion flow.

paper.title: Statistical properties of type-II bursts in Rapid Burster observed with Insight-HXMT
paper.abstract: We report the detection of type-II X-ray bursts in a neutron star low mass X-ray binary MXB 1730-335 (also known as Rapid Burster) observed with Insight-HXMT satellite. We found significant variations in the burst properties along with the decay phases of its 2017 and 2020 outbursts, such as switches between different burst modes. We investigated the statistical distributions of burst parameters (peak flux F<SUB>peak</SUB>, fluence E, burst duration t<SUB>dur</SUB>, recurrence time ∆t) and studied their correlations. We confirm the relaxation oscillator behavior (E∝∆t<SUP>α</SUP>), and find that for mode-2 bursts the index α is around 1. For mode-1 bursts, α varies with ∆t and the <mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mi>E</mml:mi><mml:mo>-</mml:mo><mml:mstyle><mml:mi>∆</mml:mi></mml:mstyle><mml:msup><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mi>α</mml:mi></mml:msup></mml:mrow></mml:math> relation can be described by a broken powerlaw model. We also confirm that F<SUB>peak</SUB> is correlated with E below a critical value and is independent of ∆t.

paper.title: A 4200-hour HyperFlash and ÉCLAT campaign on the hyperactive FRB 20240114A: constraining energetics with the most brilliant bursts
paper.abstract: Hyperactive repeaters provide a unique window into the evolving environments and energy budgets of fast radio burst (FRB) sources, though they may not be representative of the FRB population in general. High-cadence observations are key to capturing the rarest and most energetic bursts, which occur only once per hundreds to thousands of hours. Here we present an unprecedented 4, 200-hour observing campaign targeting FRB 20240114A as part of the HyperFlash and ÉCLAT FRB monitoring programs. Over 806 days, we detected 178 high-energy (~10<SUP>40 - 42</SUP> erg) bursts with HyperFlash, which together amount to 4.4 × 10<SUP>42</SUP> erg of released radio energy (assuming isotropic emission and 1-GHz emission bandwidth). The cumulative energy of the HyperFlash bursts is about twice that of ~11, 000 lower-energy bursts detected with FAST, emphasising the significant role that the highest-energy bursts play in depleting the central engine's stored energy. In fact, the single most brilliant burst from our sample, which we term the STROOP, contributes roughly 1/3 of all the energy we measure, and is at the maximum energy seen in studies of both repeating and apparently one-off FRBs alike. We also find a break in the burst energy distribution at ~2 × 10<SUP>40</SUP> erg and a linear dispersion measure (DM) increase of +0.96 ± 0.06 pc cm<SUP>-3</SUP> over a period of 318 days. We discuss these findings in the context of a magnetar source model and highlight comparisons with the energetics of intermediate and giant X-ray/γ-ray flares from Galactic sources.

paper.title: Hydrodynamic instabilities in long-term three-dimensional simulations of neutrino-driven supernovae of 13 red supergiant progenitors
paper.abstract: We present long-term three-dimensional (3D) simulations of Type-IIP supernovae (SNe) for 13 non-rotating, single-star, red-supergiant (RSG) progenitors with zero-age-main-sequence masses between 12.5 M<SUB>⊙</SUB> and 27.3 M<SUB>⊙</SUB>. The explosions were modelled with a parametric treatment of neutrino heating to obtain defined energies, <SUP>5</SUP>6Ni yields, and neutron-star properties in agreement with previous results. Our 3D SN models were evolved from core bounce until 10 days to study how the large-scale mixing of chemical elements depends on the progenitor structure. We find most extreme <SUP>5</SUP>6Ni mixing and the highest maximum <SUP>5</SUP>6Ni velocities in lower-mass (LM) explosions despite lower explosion energies, and the weakest <SUP>5</SUP>6Ni mixing in the 3D explosions of the most massive RSGs. The efficiency of radial <SUP>5</SUP>6Ni mixing anti-correlates linearly with the helium-core mass and correlates positively with the magnitude of a local maximum of ρr<SUP>3</SUP> in the helium shell. This maximum causes shock deceleration and therefore facilitates high growth factors of RTI at the (C+O)/He interface in the LM explosions. Therefore fast-moving <SUP>5</SUP>6Ni created by the asymmetric neutrino-heating mechanism is carried into the ubiquitous RT-unstable region near the He/H interface and ultimately far into the envelopes of the exploding RSGs. paper.title: Impact of Stochastic Pop III X-ray Binaries on the Cosmological 21-cm Signal
paper.abstract: High-mass X-ray binaries are one of the primary drivers of the 21-cm signal from Cosmic Dawn and Reionization, playing a leading role in the thermal history of the intergalactic medium. In traditional semi-numerical simulations, a deterministic scaling relation between the total X-ray luminosity of high-mass X-ray binaries, L<SUB>X</SUB>, and star formation rate (SFR) is usually adopted. However, this assumption is inaccurate for high-redshift low-SFR regions hosting few sources. The spatial variation in the number and luminosity of these sources is expected to enhance fluctuations in the Cosmic Dawn 21-cm signal. Here we quantify this effect by introducing a stochastic L<SUB>X</SUB> model sampled from a power-law X-ray luminosity function. Implementing this in 21cmSPACE, a large-scale simulation framework of Cosmic Dawn and Reionization, and adopting a soft X-ray spectral energy distribution (β = 1.5, E<SUB>min</SUB> = 0.1 keV) that leads to a relatively strong stochastic signature, we find that the stochasticity leads to enhanced fluctuations in X-ray heating rate fields, and affects the 21-cm power spectrum on small scales (k > 0.3 cMpc<SUP>-1</SUP>). The impact of stochasticity on the global 21-cm signal and on the large-scale power spectrum is found to be negligible. Our results suggest these effects will remain undetected by the upcoming Square Kilometer Array. However, large-scale lunar-based experiments may be sensitive to the signatures of stochastic X-ray heating at z ~ 25. Quantifying these corrections is a vital step toward robust 21-cm modeling and ensuring that future precision data interpretation is free from astrophysical biases.

paper.abstract: We present an Australian Square Kilometre Array Pathfinder (ASKAP) Evolutionary Map of the Universe (EMU) radio-continuum detection of the nearby spiral Seyfert I type galaxy NGC 7213 which we nickname `sand-timer' due to its morphological appearance. Finally, we find two previously undetected kiloparsec-scale features in the polarised intensity image, which appear most likely also related to the central SMBH, as restarted bipolar radio jets, though somewhat obscured in the radio-continuum total intensity image. They resemble the bow shocks often seen in Fanaroff-Riley Class II (FR-II) radio galaxies, and so we propose they most likely represent an early episode of the `Sand-timer's' AGN jet activity. An alternative scenario is that the core of NGC 7213 may be a super massive binary black hole (SMBBH) which is undergoing a tidal disruption event (TDE), potentially causing the peculiar radio-continuum emission.

paper.title: Optical torque reversal in the slowest accreting pulsar 4U 1954+319
paper.abstract: Wind-fed accretion onto magnetised neutron stars drives long-term spin variability that can be used to trace angular-momentum transfer in structured stellar outflows. We analyse five years of TESS optical timing to measure the spin evolution of the wind-fed X-ray pulsar 4U 1954+319, which hosts the slowest known accretion-powered pulsar. Coherent hour-scale pulsations are detected in all eight TESS sectors. The optical spin period evolves non-monotonically from 5.51±0.06 to 5.72±0.06 h and then returns to 5.55±0.05 h, consistent with a mid-2023 break and a torque reversal from spin-down to spin-up (P˙1=+0.68±0.08 s d<SUP>-1</SUP> to P˙2=-2.16±0.35 s d<SUP>-1</SUP>). The observed P˙ corresponds to torques of N<SUB>1</SUB>=(-1.2±0.1)×10<SUP>32</SUP> dyn cm and N<SUB>2</SUB>=(+3.6±0.6)×10<SUP>32</SUP> dyn cm for a canonical moment of inertia I=10<SUP>45</SUP> g cm<SUP>2</SUP>, while the associated spin-down power remains negligible compared with the X-ray luminosity. Within the quasi-spherical settling accretion regime, a change in mass accretion rate by a factor of ∼3.6 is sufficient, at the order-of-magnitude level, to account for the measured torque ratio. The inferred torque scale is compatible with a surface dipole field B≈(0.5-5)×10<SUP12</SUP< G, with the magnetospheric radius remaining well inside co-rotation and no requirement for a propeller transition at the inferred luminosities. No clear contemporaneous hard-X-ray brightening is apparent in the BAT monitoring, which is consistent with an origin of the optical pulsations in reprocessing of the pulsed high-energy emission. Overall, the data favour a picture in which 4U 1954+319 is a long-period, near-equilibrium wind-fed pulsar whose torque reversals can arise from moderate changes in settling accretion, without invoking magnetar-strength fields or persistent propeller transitions. They also show that long-baseline optical timing can provide useful constraints on torque balance in faint wind-fed pulsars.

paper.title: A PINK update: Improvements to the CELEBI fast radio burst data reduction and analysis pipeline
paper.abstract: Fast radio bursts (FRBs) which are well localised (<1″) to their host galaxy are tools for studying cosmology and the intergalactic medium. Furthermore, high-time resolution datasets of their polarisation properties can enable testing of the numerous models on their potential progenitors. To that end, the CELEBI (CRAFT Effortless Localisation and Enhanced Burst Inspection) pipeline was conceived to enable data reduction from raw antenna voltages to detect fast radio transient events, localise them to sub-arcsecond precision, and produce polarimetric data at time resolutions as fine as 3 ns. Here we present a slew of updates to the CELEBI pipeline. Improvements to the astrometry correction for FRB localisations have aided our ability to determine what part of a galaxy more nearby FRBs have occurred in, which can have its own implication on the progenitor. We also have implemented time and frequency gating on detected fast transients to enable a boost to signal-to-noise ratio, particularly useful for high dispersion measure or faint fast radio transients. We give examples of our improvements to the localisation, including for the currently `hostless' FRB 20251019A. The polarisation calibration process has been overhauled, resulting in much more accurate measurements of derived polarisation fraction and rotation measures. Furthermore, we now have incorporated tools for structure maximisation of the dispersion measure of fast radio transients, a software container which enables the installation of CELEBI on other machines, and improved the pipeline efficiency. Together these updates (named `Polarisation and astrometry Improvements for New Knowledge', or PINK) greatly improve our ability to keep up with the expected detection rate from the CRAFT COherent (CRACO) upgrade to the real-time fast transient detection system of the Australian SKA Pathfinder.

paper.title: The Lazuli Space Observatory: Opportunities for Time-domain and Multi-messenger Astronomy
paper.abstract: Advancing time-domain and multi-messenger astronomy requires a multi-wavelength network of observatories capable of rapidly discovering, classifying, and characterizing transient phenomena. A critical gap in current capabilities is the inability to follow up faint, fast-evolving transients with sensitive, wide-band imaging and spectroscopic observations from space on timescales of minutes to hours. We discuss how the Lazuli Space Observatory will address this gap through a large collecting area, optical/NIR photometry and low-resolution integral field spectroscopy, and a rapid-response architecture with a mission requirement of <4 hr from trigger to first photon. Based on a latency analysis, we find a credible path to realizing response times well below this requirement, with best-case scenarios below 90 minutes under favorable conditions. We highlight extragalactic science opportunities in currently un(der)explored parts of parameter space, including gravitational wave follow-up, kilonova characterization, supernova progenitor physics, and a wide variety of fast-evolving transients and high redshift events. We further outline new observational capabilities for Galactic time-domain science, including high frequency variability in accreting systems, precision astrometry of compact objects, and the detection of compact and ultracompact binaries, enabled by high-frequency, diffraction-limited imaging and astrometry. Together, its capabilities---combining flagship sensitivity with response times one to two orders of magnitude faster than existing large space observatories---position Lazuli to make transformative contributions across time-domain and multi-messenger astrophysics.

paper.title: Cooling of isolated neutron stars with hyperon-mixed kaon-condensation matter
paper.abstract: We investigate the thermal evolution of isolated neutron stars containing hyperon-mixed kaon-condensed matter, focusing on the role of proton superconductivity. The equation of state utilized for cooling calculation is based upon the minimal relativistic mean-field framework supplemented by chiral SU(3) dynamics for kaon condensation with an additional component on the three-baryon force, which ensures stiffness at high densities enough to meet astrophysical constraints on neutron-star masses and radii. We show that the nucleonic direct Urca processes operate at relatively low stellar masses <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mo>(</mml:mo><mml:mi>M</mml:mi><mml:mo>≳</mml:mo><mml:mn>1.3</mml:mn><mml:mspace></mml:mspace><mml:msub><mml:mi>M</mml:mi><mml:mo>⊙</mml:mo></mml:msub><mml:mo>)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:math></inline-formula>, erasing any observable signature of strangeness in the absence of superfluidity. However, if the proton <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:msup><mml:mrow></mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:msup><mml:msub><mml:mi>S</mml:mi><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:math></inline-formula> superconductivity works, because of suppression of fast neutrino cooling processes, the cooling scenario could become relevant with the strangeness, depending on the density regions of the pairing gap. In particular, if the proton superconductivity is so strong in high-density regions <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mo>(</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mi>T</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mi>c</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>~</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mn>10</mml:mn><mml:mn>10</mml:mn></mml:msup><mml:mspace></mml:mspace><mml:mi>K</mml:mi><mml:mo>)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:math></inline-formula>, the nucleon and hyperon direct Urca processes shut down, which makes the kaon-induced Urca processes dominant in massive neutron stars. This scenario is in good agreement with several cold isolated neutron stars identified recently, such as the Vela Jr., PSR <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mn>0205</mml:mn><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:mn>6449</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:math></inline-formula>, and PSR B2334 <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mo>+</mml:mo></mml:math></inline-formula> 61. Hence, we suggest that strong proton superconductivity can render kaon condensation observationally visible through cold neutron-star observations, providing a potential signature of strangeness in dense matter.

paper.title: Impact of soft versus hard equations of state on hybrid stars
paper.abstract: The nuclear stiffness as a dominant contribution of nuclear symmetry energy is analyzed in the context of the properties of compact stars, considering constraints from nuclear physics and astrophysics. A compact star can be a neutron star composed only of nuclear matter or a hybrid star with a quark core. Two typical models (soft and stiff) are considered for the nuclear equation of state and for the hybrid equation of state, and a parametrized first-order phase-transition approach completed with a linear quark-matter equation of state is implemented. We show that the phase transition reduces the tension between GW170817 and NICER observations, and we illustrate how the nuclear stiffness affects the understanding of the nature of the binary system in GW170817. The implication for nuclear symmetry energy is also discussed. We also confirm our previous findings that the GW170817 waveform is best described as a binary hybrid star with a low-density onset of stiff quark matter. This could also be interpreted as a quarkyonic crossover.

paper.title: Impact of the Einstein Telescope's duty cycle on the estimation of binary black hole parameters
paper.abstract: The geometry of the Einstein Telescope, the proposed next-generation European gravitational-wave observatory, is yet to be finalized. Two competing designs are under consideration: a nested triangular configuration (ET-<inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mi>∆</mml:mi></mml:math></inline-formula>) and two separated <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mi>L</mml:mi></mml:math></inline-formula>-shaped detectors (ET-2L). Extensive prior comparisons of ET designs established the scientific landscape using the Fisher-information-matrix formalism and identified that duty-cycle-induced single-detector operation is precisely the regime where this approximation becomes less reliable, underscoring the need for a refined, principled treatment of the duty cycle. In this manuscript, we build on that foundation by revisiting the comparison with full Bayesian parameter estimation of gravitational-wave signals from binary black hole mergers, projected onto a simulated Einstein Telescope that incorporates a refined duty cycle modeled via continuous-time Markov chains and testing different detector maintenance strategies. We find that the redundancy inherent in the ET-<inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mi>∆</mml:mi></mml:math></inline-formula> design enables it to maintain at least two operational detectors for the majority of the observing time, whereas the ET-2L configuration is often limited to a single detector. Crucially, we show that, during partial network operation, ET-<inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mi>∆</mml:mi></mml:math></inline-formula> often outperforms ET-2L, and that the increased multidetector uptime translates into tighter constraints on the luminosity distance and source-frame component masses. Notably, this remains true even when gravitational-wave events have a lower signal-to-noise ratio in ET-<inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mi>∆</mml:mi></mml:math></inline-formula> than in ET-2L.

paper.title: Time-domain synthesis of gravitational-wave detector glitches using class-conditional derivative generative adversarial networks
paper.abstract: Gravitational-wave detectors such as LIGO, Virgo, and KAGRA are highly sensitive instruments susceptible to numerous noise sources. Short-duration transient noise events, known as glitches, pose a particular challenge for data analysis pipelines as they can mimic or obscure astrophysical signals. We present GlitchGAN, a class-conditional generative model, built upon the conditional derivative GAN (cDVGAN) architecture, that is capable of synthesizing glitches directly in the time domain. The model is trained on high-quality reconstructions of seven common glitch types observed during LIGO's third observing run (O3): blip, fast scattering, koi fish, low-frequency burst, scattered light, tomte, and whistle. We show that GlitchGAN generalizes effectively, learning to reproduce a diverse glitch space that is consistent with these reconstructions. Moreover, because the model is conditioned on glitch class, it can generate hybrid or transitional glitch morphologies by interpolating across the class-conditioning vector after training. GlitchGAN generates 1000 glitches in under 22 seconds on a CPU, making it suitable for large-scale glitch synthesis for detector simulations, mock data challenges, and pipeline validation. Synthetic glitches are validated against real glitch reconstructions using the Gravity Spy classifier, widely used in the GW community for glitch classification, and an unsupervised analysis using UMAP embeddings. Gravity Spy classifies the majority of GlitchGAN's synthetic glitches as the correct class while the UMAP analysis shows substantial overlap between real and synthetic samples in the reduced latent space. To investigate residual distributional differences between real glitches unseen during training and generated synthetic glitches, we train a separate holdout GlitchGAN model on nearly the same dataset but with a small held-out split, and use a downstream convolutional neural network to distinguish these held-out real glitches from synthetic glitches produced by the holdout model. While this classifier reliably detects synthetic samples in a clean, noise-free representation, this detectability drops substantially once real and synthetic glitches are injected into realistic detector noise, the condition under which synthetic glitches would typically be deployed for downstream applications. Despite remaining statistically distinguishable, we show that GlitchGAN-generated glitches are practically useful: augmenting real training datasets with synthetic samples matches simple duplication of the same real data when data is abundant, and increasingly outperforms it as real data becomes scarcer. Finally, we highlight a critical limitation of magnitude-only spectrograms: classifiers operating on magnitude <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mi>Q</mml:mi></mml:math></inline-formula>-transforms can confidently misclassify physically unrealistic glitches from less robust models, underscoring the need for complementary validation methods that preserve phase information.

paper.abstract: The coalescence of degenerate helium cores during red giant collisions---a process we term ``erythrohenosis''---introduces a novel class of transient astrophysical sources of high-energy neutrinos. Using stellar models generated with MESA and smoothed-particle hydrodynamics simulations of the final inspiral phase, we develop a semianalytical model to estimate the amount of hydrogen mixed into the cores, the energy release (<inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mo>≈</mml:mo><mml:mn>4.28</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mn>10</mml:mn><mml:mn>49</mml:mn></mml:msup><mml:mtext> </mml:mtext><mml:mtext> </mml:mtext><mml:mi>erg</mml:mi></mml:math></inline-formula>) that heats the remnant to <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mi>T</mml:mi><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:msub><mml:mo>≈</mml:mo><mml:mn>5.3</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mn>10</mml:mn><mml:mn>8</mml:mn></mml:msup><mml:mtext> </mml:mtext><mml:mtext> </mml:mtext><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:math></inline-formula>, the magnetic field amplification (<inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mi>B</mml:mi><mml:mo>≈</mml:mo><mml:mn>1.77</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mn>10</mml:mn><mml:mn>10</mml:mn></mml:msup><mml:mtext> </mml:mtext><mml:mtext> </mml:mtext><mml:mi>G</mml:mi></mml:math></inline-formula>), and the resulting neutrino flux. The predicted TeV--PeV neutrino signal may contribute to the diffuse IceCube neutrino flux; we estimate that the horizon at which a single neutrino event is expected on average at <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mo>≳</mml:mo><mml:mn>100</mml:mn><mml:mtext> </mml:mtext><mml:mtext> </mml:mtext><mml:mi>TeV</mml:mi></mml:math></inline-formula> is <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mo>≈</mml:mo><mml:mn>55</mml:mn><mml:mtext> </mml:mtext><mml:mtext> </mml:mtext><mml:mi>kpc</mml:mi></mml:math></inline-formula> for individual merger events. Furthermore, we discuss the probability of a magnetized helium flash and assess the subsequent activation of the CNO cycle in the remnant core due to hydrogen mixing. In particular, neutrinos from the decay of <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mmultiscripts><mml:mrow><mml:mi>F</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>18</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mmultiscripts></mml:mrow></mml:math></inline-formula> offer a direct observational test of the detonation, (as sources within <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mo>~</mml:mo><mml:mn>4.4</mml:mn><mml:mtext> </mml:mtext><mml:mtext> </mml:mtext><mml:mi>pc</mml:mi></mml:math></inline-formula> would produce a neutrino flux exceeding the solar CNO neutrino background). The simultaneous emission of high-energy hadronic neutrinos, gravitational waves, and---if the optical depth permits (<inline-formula><mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mi>τ</mml:mi><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:msub><mml:mo>~</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mn>10</mml:mn><mml:mn>14</mml:mn></mml:msup></mml:math></inline-formula> in the core of the remnant)---an electromagnetic signal would constitute a unique multimessenger signature of red giant core collisions, positioning erythrohenosis events as exotic yet potentially observable phenomena in dense stellar systems.

paper.abstract: The composition and properties of infinite nuclear matter under extreme conditions of temperature and pressure remain incompletely understood. In this work, we constrain the equation of state (EoS) of nuclear matter---constructed within the framework of the relativistic mean field (RMF) model---by combining results from chiral effective field theory and multimessenger observations of neutron stars. Using the saturation properties of nuclear matter, we generate a wide ensemble of EoS, which are subsequently constrained within a Bayesian framework. The resulting posterior distributions provide tight bounds on both the saturation parameters and the coupling constants of the RMF model. The radius of a <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mn>1.4</mml:mn><mml:msub><mml:mi>M</mml:mi><mml:mo>⊙</mml:mo></mml:msub></mml:math></inline-formula> neutron star is tightly constrained to <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mn>12.471</mml:mn><mml:mrow><mml:mo>-</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.394</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.427</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mtext> </mml:mtext><mml:mtext> </mml:mtext><mml:mi>km</mml:mi></mml:math></inline-formula>, while the maximum mass reaches <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:msubsup><mml:mn>2.156</mml:mn><mml:mrow><mml:mo>-</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.120</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.175</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:msub><mml:mi>M</mml:mi><mml:mo>⊙</mml:mo></mml:msub></mml:math></inline-formula>. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that the <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi><mml:mi>--</mml:mi><mml:mi>ρ</mml:mi></mml:math></inline-formula> coupling, which governs the density dependence of the symmetry energy, becomes increasingly significant under successive astrophysical constraints. Finally, the predicted <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>skin</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:math></inline-formula> of <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mmultiscripts><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Ca</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>48</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mmultiscripts></mml:mrow></mml:math></inline-formula> agrees well with the CREX measurement, whereas that of <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mmultiscripts><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Pb</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>208</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mmultiscripts></mml:mrow></mml:math></inline-formula> remains in tension with PREX-II. In contrast to earlier studies, we do not observe a clear correlation between the <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>skin</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:math></inline-formula> of <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mmultiscripts><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Pb</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>208</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mmultiscripts></mml:mrow></mml:math></inline-formula> and the symmetry energy slope parameter <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mi>L</mml:mi></mml:math></inline-formula>.

paper.title: Multimessenger detectability of continuous gravitational waves from the near future to next generation detectors
paper.abstract: Continuous gravitational waves have the potential to transform gravitational wave astronomy and yield fresh insights into astrophysics, nuclear and particle physics, and condensed matter physics. We evaluate their detectability by combining various theoretical and observational arguments from the literature and systematically applying those arguments to known astronomical objects and future gravitational wave detectors. We detail and update previous estimates made in support of Cosmic Explorer [Evans et al., arXiv:2306.13745 and Gupta et al., Classical Quantum Gravity 41, 245001 (2024)CQGRDG0264-938110.1088/1361-6382/ad7b99]. It is commonly argued that the spins of accreting neutron stars are regulated by gravitational wave emission and that millisecond pulsars contain a young pulsar's magnetic field buried under accreted material. If either of these arguments holds, the first detection of continuous gravitational waves is likely with near future upgrades of current detectors, and many detections are likely with next generation detectors such as Cosmic Explorer and the Einstein Telescope. A lack of detections in the next several years would begin to raise serious doubts about current theories of millisecond pulsar formation.

A species-resolved Ledoux decomposition, cross-checked through mode-frequency sensitivities, identifies the driving channels. Fast-<inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:math></inline-formula> equilibration retains 36%--44% of the peak local value of <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>c</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>s</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mo>-</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>c</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>e</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup></mml:mrow></mml:math></inline-formula>. paper.title: Isolated or dynamical? Tracing black hole binary formation through the population of gravitational-wave sources
paper.abstract: The population of binary black hole (BBH) mergers observed by the LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA (LVK) collaboration offers a window into the cosmic evolution of compact binaries and the physical mechanisms that drive their formation. We employ the semianalytic population-synthesis code B-POP to model BBHs assembled through isolated binary evolution and dynamical interactions in young, globular, and nuclear star clusters. Our framework self-consistently incorporates star formation history, metallicity evolution, and single and binary stellar evolution to quantify their impact on the observable properties of the BBH population and on the relative contribution of distinct formation channels. Our models are characterized by a merger rate, <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mi>R</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>17.5</mml:mn><mml:mi>--</mml:mi><mml:mn>24.1</mml:mn><mml:mtext> </mml:mtext><mml:mtext> </mml:mtext><mml:msup><mml:mi>Gpc</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo>-</mml:mo><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mtext> </mml:mtext><mml:mtext> </mml:mtext><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>yr</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>-</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math></inline-formula>, broadly consistent with LVK constraints. Moreover, the predicted distributions of primary mass, mass ratio, and effective inspiral spin parameter are compatible with those inferred from current LVK observations. paper.title: Consistency of standard cosmologies using Bayesian model comparison and tension quantification
paper.abstract: We present a unified Bayesian assessment of model comparison and dataset consistency for <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mi>Λ</mml:mi><mml:mi>CDM</mml:mi></mml:math></inline-formula> (cold dark matter plus a cosmological constant) and minimal extensions (neutrino mass, spatial curvature, and constant or evolving dark energy) using cosmic microwave background (CMB), baryon acoustic oscillation (BAO), and type Ia supernova (SN) data. The major results are summarized in the first three figures. We quantify model preference with Bayesian evidence and assess consistency with complementary evidence- and likelihood-based diagnostics applied uniformly across dataset combinations. For the models considered, updated PLANCK processing systematically improves internal CMB consistency (low-<inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mo>ℓ</mml:mo></mml:math></inline-formula> versus high-<inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mo>ℓ</mml:mo></mml:math></inline-formula>, and primary CMB versus CMB lensing). The preference for a closed geometry and an associated ``curvature tension'' with BAO and/or CMB lensing are largely confined to earlier PLANCK likelihood implementations and weaken substantially when using updated CMB processing and more recent BAO measurements. Apparent evidence for evolving dark energy in <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mi>CMB</mml:mi><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:mi>BAO</mml:mi><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:mi>SN</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:math></inline-formula> combinations depends sensitively on the specific pairing of CMB and SN likelihoods: plausible alternatives shift inferred tensions by more than <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:math></inline-formula> and can completely reverse the preferred model. Allowing a free neutrino mass tends to absorb residual shifts without introducing new inconsistencies, and we do not find robust evidence for a standalone <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mi>τ</mml:mi></mml:math></inline-formula>-driven discrepancy once the full likelihood context is accounted for. We conclude that claims of a required update of our standard cosmological model from <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mi>Λ</mml:mi><mml:mi>CDM</mml:mi></mml:math></inline-formula> to <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mi>w</mml:mi><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mi>w</mml:mi><mml:mi>a</mml:mi></mml:msub><mml:mi>CDM</mml:mi></mml:math></inline-formula> are premature.

paper.title: Static spherically symmetric Kundt vacuum solutions of higher-derivative gravities
paper.abstract: We study static spherically symmetric Kundt solutions to the vacuum field equations of quadratic gravity with a cosmological constant, as well as specific models of six-derivative gravity. In quadratic gravity, we identify all solutions for coupling constants satisfying <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mi>α</mml:mi><mml:mo>!=</mml:mo><mml:mn>3</mml:mn><mml:mi>β</mml:mi></mml:math></inline-formula>, while the case <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mi>α</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>3</mml:mn><mml:mi>β</mml:mi></mml:math></inline-formula> is studied using the Frobenius method, where we derive the recurrence relations for the power series. In contrast, in six-derivative gravity, we focus on selected models to illustrate the variety of closed-form solutions; we also analyze possible indicial families of Frobenius solutions. For all solutions, we analyze curvature singularities and their accessibility to geodesic observers. We then construct exact gravitational-wave solutions propagating on some of these backgrounds in quadratic and six-derivative gravity. It is known that in Einstein gravity, gravitational waves on the Nariai background unavoidably contain singularities, which are interpreted as physical sources generating these gravitational waves. In contrast, in addition to singular solutions, for appropriate values of the coupling constants, higher-order gravities allow for globally smooth solutions representing gravitational waves.

paper.title: Properties of natural polynomials for Schwarzschild and Kerr black holes
paper.abstract: The quasinormal modes of black holes play various important roles in gravitational wave theory, signal modeling, and data analysis; however, there remain open questions about their mathematical properties. Aspects of classical polynomial theory have been proposed as a framework to investigate quasinormal mode orthogonality and completeness. We have recently presented a class of polynomials that are ``natural'' to quasinormal modes in that they are restricted by the quasinormal mode boundary conditions, and exactly tridiagonalize Teukolsky's radial equation. In turn, these polynomials may be useful for (i) better understanding the vector space properties of quasinormal mode solutions (ii) serving as a basis for spectral methods to solve the Teukolsky and confluent Heun equations. Here, we provide an overview of these polynomials' basic analytic properties: their three-term recurrence relation, ladder operators, and governing differential equation. We demonstrate that the natural polynomials for Schwarzschild and Kerr black holes are Pollaczek-Jacobi polynomials with complex valued parameters. We verify that, despite being constrained to the real line, key results for Pollaczek-Jacobi polynomials hold for black hole polynomials. Along the way, we observe a novel property that is particular to Schwarzschild: the polynomials' three-term recurrence relation always peaks at the physical overtone index. This work supports the broader application of these polynomials to spectral methods for solving the Teukolsky equation, and other instances of the confluent Heun equation.

paper.title: Fast neural network surrogate for multimodal effective-one-body gravitational waveforms from generically precessing compact binaries
paper.abstract: Gravitational waveform templates are a key ingredient for the detection and characterization of gravitational waves emitted by compact binary mergers in the Universe. These templates must be physically accurate and extensive, but also highly computationally efficient, two requirements that are often in tension. One solution to this problem is the development of surrogate models, which are fast, data-driven models trained to predict the output of a slower, physically realistic waveform model. In this article we build on existing work to incorporate machine learning techniques into the conventional reduced order surrogate framework, with a focus on extending coverage to waveform models that describe generically precessing quasicircular binaries. In particular, we present SEOBNRv5PHM_NNSur7dq10, a reduced order neural network surrogate of the SEOBNRv5PHM waveform model, valid up to mass ratios <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mo>∶</mml:mo><mml:mn>10</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:math></inline-formula> for precessing quasicircular binary black hole systems with arbitrary spin magnitudes and orientations. The faithfulness of the surrogate to SEOBNRv5PHM is validated, and the surrogate is successfully applied to Bayesian parameter inference using both real and injected gravitational wave data. The surrogate is approximately five times faster than SEOBNRv5PHM when evaluating a single waveform on a central processing unit, and nearly 1000 times faster per waveform when amortizing the cost over large waveform batches on a graphics processing unit.

paper.title: Gravitational light deflection and shadows in a warm plasma
paper.abstract: Analytical studies of light bending in a dispersive medium near compact objects, e.g., black holes or neutron stars, are most challenged by a suitable definition of the medium. The most realistic model would be a hot magnetized plasma. In such a medium, however, an analytical description of light rays is very difficult. Therefore, usually an isotropic dispersive medium is assumed in analytical calculations. While it is possible to formulate equations for a general refractive index, which some studies do, most attention in the literature is given to the particular case of a cold, nonmagnetized electron-ion plasma. Whereas this model covers many astrophysically relevant situations, there are indications that in some cases the plasma temperature is so high that the approximation of a cold plasma is no longer valid. For this reason, we consider in this paper a warm, nonmagnetized electron-ion plasma, where the temperature is not set equal to zero but assumed to be small enough, such that relevant equations can be linearized with respect to it. After discussing the general equations for light rays in such a medium on a general-relativistic spacetime, we specify to the axially symmetric and stationary case which includes the spherically symmetric and static case. In particular, we calculate the influence of a warm plasma on the bending angle. In the spherically symmetric and static case, we also calculate the shadow in a warm plasma. We illustrate the general results with a static (respectively corotating) and an infalling warm plasma on Schwarzschild and Kerr spacetimes.

paper.title: Gravitational synchronization in bosonic dark matter admixed neutron stars
paper.abstract: While the search for dark matter remains a central focus of modern astrophysics and high-energy physics, neutron stars could provide natural laboratories in which the interaction between dark matter and baryonic matter can be studied. In this work, we model dark matter as an ultralight bosonic field, which can accrete onto the neutron star and form a composite object bound through gravity. Using long-term, numerical relativity simulations in spherical symmetry, we extract and analyze the frequency spectra of the radial oscillation modes of fermion-boson stars. Our simulations reveal that the fermionic and bosonic components synchronize through gravitational coupling regardless of the equation of state, enriching their oscillation spectrum. This synchronization leads to new multistate scalar configurations and reshapes the hierarchy of the neutron-star radial modes. We further propose a procedure to compute the values of the new dominant modes as a function of the bosonic mass and discuss how the synchronization mechanism extends beyond spherical symmetry together with its implications for neutron-star physics and gravitational-wave astronomy.

paper.title: Neutrino Emissivity in <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mi>∆</mml:mi></mml:math></inline-formula>-Direct-Urca Processes Inside Neutron Stars
paper.abstract: Observed massive neutron stars may contain heavier baryons such as <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mi>∆</mml:mi></mml:math></inline-formula> isobars and hyperons in their interiors. In the presence of <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mi>∆</mml:mi></mml:math></inline-formula> isobars, the neutrino emitting nucleonic Urca processes can be accompanied by <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mi>∆</mml:mi></mml:math></inline-formula>-direct-Urca processes involving nucleons and hyperons. Over the past three decades, significant theoretical effort has been dedicated to understanding the thermal evolution of neutron stars with the nucleonic and hyperonic Urca processes emerging as dominant cooling mechanisms. While recent studies have proposed the presence of <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mi>∆</mml:mi></mml:math></inline-formula> isobars in the dense core of neutron stars, the specific contribution of the <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mi>∆</mml:mi></mml:math></inline-formula>-direct-Urca process to neutrino emissivity has not been explicitly quantified. In this Letter, we address this gap by deriving the neutrino emissivity associated with <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mi>∆</mml:mi></mml:math></inline-formula>-direct-Urca processes in dense matter inside neutron stars. We show that once <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mi>∆</mml:mi></mml:math></inline-formula>-direct-Urca processes become kinematically allowed, their emissivities are comparable to those of nucleonic-direct-Urca processes.

paper.title: Multi-Wavelength View of a Confined C2.2 Flare: From Compact Two-Ribbon Emission to a Tailed C-Shaped Ribbon Morphology
paper.abstract: Flare ribbon morphology is often used as an observational proxy for magnetic reconnection and the underlying coronal magnetic topology. However, complex ribbon shapes do not necessarily imply a specific large-scale topology, particularly when different atmospheric diagnostics sample different parts of the same event. We examine this problem using an apparently confined C2.2 flare in NOAA active region (AR) 13078 on 2022 August 16, observed with the Solar Dynamics Observatory/Atmospheric Imaging Assembly (SDO/AIA), Solar Dynamics Observatory/Helioseismic and Magnetic Imager (SDO/HMI), New Vacuum Solar Telescope (NVST) H<inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mi>α</mml:mi></mml:math></inline-formula> imaging, and a non-force-free Field (NFFF) extrapolation. The flare shows a strongly wavelength-dependent ribbon morphology. In lower-atmospheric diagnostics, especially AIA 1600 Å and NVST H<inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mi>α</mml:mi></mml:math></inline-formula>, it appears mainly as a compact two-ribbon flare rooted around a polarity inversion line (PIL). In contrast, AIA 304 Å reveals a C-shaped ribbon with an extended tail linking the compact flaring core to nearby pores and plage. The extended AIA 304 Å morphology appears to develop through the progressive brightening of connected, low-lying magnetic loops, rather than representing a separate ribbon system. The pre-flare phase shows localized ultraviolet (UV)/extreme-ultraviolet (EUV) brightenings together with loops in hot AIA channels. Hot AIA channels reveal a sigmoid-like structure associated with the same low-lying magnetic system that hosts the active-region filament and nearby arch filament system. During the flare, the H<inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mi>α</mml:mi></mml:math></inline-formula> filamentary material becomes less visible in places, most likely due to heating, enhanced background emission, and opacity changes, rather than complete disappearance or eruption. The extrapolated field contains a coronal null point at higher altitude; however, its fan and spine footpoints are not co-spatial with the observed flare ribbons or with the extended tail brightening. This suggests that the large-scale null-point topology is unlikely to be the primary cause of the C-shaped ribbon morphology. Nevertheless, the extrapolation does reproduce the low-lying magnetic connectivity associated with the active-region filament, the arch filament system, and loops linking the positive-polarity sunspot to surrounding negative-polarity pores and plage. Together, the observations and extrapolated magnetic field topology support a scenario in which the extended tail of the C-shaped ribbon results from the progressive formation or successive heating of the loops connecting the sunspot and plage, rather than from reconnection at the higher coronal null.

paper.title: Simulating eccentric binary black hole signals: a PyCBC study of waveform morphology and matched-filter performance
paper.abstract: Searches for gravitational waves from compact binary coalescences usually rely on template banks that assume the binaries are on nearly circular orbits. In contrast, systems assembled through dynamical capture or in very dense stellar environments can retain significant orbital eccentricity, producing signal shapes that are poorly matched by these standard ``matched-filter searches''. This study investigates how orbital eccentricity alters both waveform structure and detection performance for three binary black hole systems: an equal-mass (30,30) <mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mi>M</mml:mi><mml:mo>⊙</mml:mo></mml:msub><mml:mspace></mml:mspace></mml:mrow></mml:math>a highly asymmetric (30,10)<mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mi>M</mml:mi><mml:mo>⊙</mml:mo></mml:msub></mml:math>, and a moderately asymmetric (70,30) <mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mi>M</mml:mi><mml:mo>⊙</mml:mo></mml:msub><mml:mspace></mml:mspace></mml:mrow></mml:math>configuration. Time-domain gravitational wave signals are produced with the EccentricTD approximant implemented in PyCBC over a range of eccentricities, then injected into stationary Gaussian noise coloured by the aLIGO Zero Detuned High Power sensitivity curve. The noisy data are processed with matched filtering using standard quasi-circular SEOBNRv4_opt templates. Results show that higher eccentricity generates waveforms with larger peak strain, more pronounced chirp modulations, and substantially reduced durations. At large eccentricities, the matched-filter SNR shows a clear but non-monotonic drop, driven mainly by waveform dephasing and the consequent loss of overlap between eccentric signals and circular templates, with the most severe impact seen for the high-mass asymmetric configuration. A comparison with data from GW150914 serves as a qualitative sanity check for the circular waveform model used for this event and illustrates that the data-conditioning workflow maintains the essential signal morphology, while the eccentric simulations highlight how even moderate eccentricity can produce waveforms that depart sharply from the quasi-circular chirp seen in current detections.

paper.title: Limit on high energy neutrino emission from Abell 119 using IceCube 10-year muon track data
paper.abstract: We carry out a search for high energy muon neutrino emission from the galaxy cluster Abell 119, motivated by a recent tentative detection of GeV gamma-ray emission from this cluster using the Fermi-LAT telescope, which hinted at a hadronic origin. For this purpose, we used the 10-year muon track data from 2008--2018, provided by the IceCube Collaboration and implement the unbinned maximum likelihood method. We do not find any statistically significant excess and the observed value of the test statistic is consistent with a null result. We then obtain upper limits (at 90% confidence level) on the differential muon neutrino energy flux from this cluster, whose value is equal to <mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1.2</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>-</mml:mo><mml:mn>9</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mspace></mml:mspace><mml:mi>GeV</mml:mi><mml:mspace></mml:mspace><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>cm</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>-</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mspace></mml:mspace><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>s</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>-</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow></mml:math> at a pivot energy of 100 TeV, after assuming a neutrino spectral index of 2.0. The neutrino flux expected under the hadronic interpretation is, however, approximately an order of magnitude smaller than our flux limit, and hence the hadronic model cannot be ruled out based on our upper limit. Among the next generation neutrino detectors, IceCube-Gen2 and TRIDENT neutrino detector should be able to confirm or rule out a hadronic origin for the gamma-ray emission in Abell 119 with 10 years of exposure.

Just 256 and 1041 are experimental α and <mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mi>β</mml:mi><mml:mo>-</mml:mo></mml:msup></mml:math> decay rates, respectively, indicating a strong dependence of heating rates on theoretical decay rates. With the data complemented by theoretical rates for the cases where data are not available, it has been found that the heating rate, <mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mover><mml:mrow><mml:mi>∊</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo>˙</mml:mo></mml:mover><mml:mrow><mml:mo>(</mml:mo><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo>)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mrow></mml:math>, shows deviations over time from the commonly assumed power-law behavior, <mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mover><mml:mrow><mml:mi>∊</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo>˙</mml:mo></mml:mover><mml:mrow><mml:mo>(</mml:mo><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo>)</mml:mo></mml:mrow><mml:mo>∝</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mo>-</mml:mo><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow></mml:math>, where x typically ranges between 1 and 1.4. Small fluctuations from the power-law behavior of <mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mover><mml:mrow><mml:mi>∊</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mo>˙</mml:mo></mml:mover><mml:mrow><mml:mo>(</mml:mo><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mo>)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mrow></mml:math> can lead to bumps in the luminosity curves at specific times. The latter can be related to the decays of a few nuclear species that contribute significantly at late times. paper.title: Study of pulse jitter characteristics of PSR J1744 - 1134: Towards high precision pulsar timing with InPTA
paper.abstract: Variations in the shapes of individual pulses introduce a broadband noise component in pulsar times of arrival beyond what is expected from radiometer noise, referred to as the jitter noise. This noise limits the timing accuracy and, consequently, the sensitivity required for the detection of nanohertz gravitational waves using pulsar timing arrays. Accurate characterization of jitter noise, including its amplitude and frequency dependence, is therefore essential for each pulsar. In this work, we present the first detailed study of jitter noise in PSR J1744 - 1134 over the frequency range 300--500 MHz, using observations from the Indian Pulsar Timing Array experiment conducted with the upgraded Giant Metrewave Radio Telescope. We detect clear signatures of jitter in this pulsar through pulse-level analysis and Bayesian inference. Furthermore, we investigated the frequency dependence of the jitter noise and compared our results with earlier measurements at higher frequencies. The observed differences in jitter amplitude suggest a possible frequency evolution, highlighting the importance of low-frequency studies for improving pulsar timing precision and accuracy. We also investigated the effect of jitter on the high precision dispersion measure derived from our observations and found that jitter is not the limiting factor for DM precision achieved for this pulsar in the given observation timescale.

paper.title: The maximum neutron-star mass from a cumulant equation of state: Coherence structure, a microscopic foundation to twice saturation, and the super-conformal core demanded by observation

We build the star from this engine with no input from observation: the cumulant EOS is computed to <mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mn>10</mml:mn><mml:mspace></mml:mspace><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>n</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:math>, taken to <mml:math><mml:mi>β</mml:mi></mml:math>-equilibrium with empirical symmetric matter (symmetry energy 38 MeV, slope 59 MeV, the latter consistent with ab initio values) and solved for the stellar structure. paper.title: Rotating Dunkl black holes in a cloud of strings confronted with M87*, Sgr A* and three X-ray binaries
paper.abstract: Rotating regular black holes (BHs) share a signature: their effective source obeys the null and weak energy conditions everywhere and breaks the dominant one only inside a compact core. We ask whether an algebraically non-local deformation reproduces that pattern. The charged Dunkl metric function of Baddis et al. extended by a Letelier cloud of strings, is rotated with the Azreg-Aïnou modified Newman--Janis algorithm, and we read the matter content off the Einstein tensor so that the analysis rests on the ordinary field equations rather than on the Dunkl-modified operators that motivate the seed. The effective mass function splits into three powers of <mml:math><mml:mi>r</mml:mi></mml:math>, carrying the string deficit, the Dunkl-renormalized mass and the Coulomb term. Conservation follows from the contracted Bianchi identity, and symbolic and numerical checks confirm the curvature invariants and every stress--energy component. The pattern is not reproduced. The strong energy condition fails on the whole scanned domain and the null, weak and dominant conditions over most of it, so the source is phantom-like rather than regular. A horizon survives up to a ceiling on the string density, with no closed timelike curves outside it. Event Horizon Telescope diameters bound both deformation parameters, and a precession fit to twin oscillations returns a Dunkl parameter near 0.3 in three X-ray binaries.

paper.title: Black hole shadows and weak gravitational lensing in charged bumblebee gravity: Plasma effects and EHT constraints
paper.abstract: We investigate photon motion, black-hole shadows, weak gravitational lensing, and image magnification for a charged static black hole in bumblebee gravity immersed in dispersive plasma environments. The bumblebee field introduces spontaneous Lorentz-symmetry breaking through the dimensionless parameter <mml:math><mml:mi>L</mml:mi></mml:math>, while the electric charge is characterized by <mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Q</mml:mi><mml:mo>/</mml:mo><mml:mi>M</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:math>. Photon propagation is treated with the Hamiltonian formalism for a cold non-magnetized plasma. A homogeneous plasma and a non-uniform power-law profile are used in the photon-sphere and shadow analyses, while homogeneous and singular-isothermal-sphere (SIS) plasmas are considered in the weak-lensing analysis We first determine the allowed black-hole domain from the horizon condition and then compute the photon-sphere radius, optical shadow radius, EHT-compatible angular shadow size, weak deflection angle, and magnification observables. The results show that increasing the charge-to-mass ratio decreases the photon-sphere and shadow radii and suppresses the weak deflection angle, while the Lorentz-violating parameter produces a milder but systematic reduction of these observables through its coupling to the charge sector. Plasma dispersion shifts the photon sphere outward but reduces the apparent shadow radius; in contrast, its effect on weak lensing depends on the plasma profile, enhancing the homogeneous-plasma deflection while slightly suppressing the SIS-plasma deflection. We further confront the theoretical shadow with the Event Horizon Telescope measurements of M87* and Sgr A*. The EHT angular diameters, <mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>M87∗</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>42</mml:mn><mml:mo>±</mml:mo><mml:mn>3</mml:mn><mml:mspace></mml:mspace><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:mi>as</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:math> and <mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Sgr A∗</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>48.7</mml:mn><mml:mo>±</mml:mo><mml:mn>7</mml:mn><mml:mspace></mml:mspace><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:mi>as</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:math>, translate into exclusion regions in the <mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mo>(</mml:mo><mml:mi>L</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>Q</mml:mi><mml:mo>/</mml:mo><mml:mi>M</mml:mi><mml:mo>)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:math> parameter space and show that charge, Lorentz violation, and plasma dispersion are strongly degenerate in shadow-based tests. These results demonstrate that simultaneous use of shadow constraints, weak deflection, and magnification can provide complementary probes of Lorentz-violating charged black-hole spacetimes in realistic plasma environments.

paper.title: Five-layer anisotropic compact stars with a generalized Chaplygin core and modified polytropic layers

paper.title: Lunar tidal response-induced clock frequency variations on the Moon
paper.abstract: As clock performance improves, the instability and uncertainty of the clock's fractional frequency shift (FFS) become comparable to the FFS caused by the lunar tidal response (LTR), so the influence of the LTR on lunar time needs to be investigated. In this paper, we used the Keplerian expansions method to study the FFS to the level of $10^{-18}$ caused by the LTR between two clocks placed in different positions on the Moon. We consider the case of the Moon orbiting in an elliptical orbit, which is closer to the actual situation compared to the case of the Moon moving in a circular orbit. An interesting phenomenon is found that the longitude difference between two clocks can cause a change in the amplitude and phase of the FFS due to the LTR, but the latitude difference only changes the amplitude of the FFS. We further estimated the clock difference between two clocks near the Moon caused by the LTR. When one clock is on the lunar surface, and the other is on the Earth's surface, the LTR will cause a clock difference of $% -5.68\times 10^{-7}$ $μ$s/day between the two clocks. These are significant for the construction of a lunar time and clock synchronization near the Moon.

paper.title: On the Doppler Effect in Static Materials: Vortices and Black, White and Worm-Hole Like Wave Trajectories
paper.abstract: We demonstrate the Doppler effect in a static material. The effect is achieved with a network of thin waveguides whose lengths depend on the direction of travel, chosen to simulate the compression and expansion of the wave experienced by a source travelling with velocity $v$. Each edge of length $\ell$ becomes a pair of waveguides of lengths $\ell/(1\mp v/c)$, one for each direction of travel. On a lattice this gives the field pattern of a moving source. To demonstrate the effect, we design a vortex, an analogue black hole and wormhole.

paper.title: Observational constraints on a non-minimally coupled scalar field in non-metricity gravity with an extra degree of freedom
paper.abstract: We investigate a non-minimally coupled scalar field in non-metricity gravity, adopting a non-trivial connection class in spatially flat FLRW spacetimes. In contrast to the coincident-gauge choice, this connection class activates an additional dynamical degree of freedom (DoF) that modifies the background evolution. We study two representative models, defined by power-law and exponential coupling functions with the exponential potential for scalar field. Confronting both models with recent combined datasets - DESI BAO, two independent supernova compilations, and cosmic chronometers - we find that each reproduces an extended matter-dominated era followed by a stable late-time de-Sitter attractor, with inferred parameters consistent with the standard $Λ$CDM model. A complementary autonomous dynamical-system analysis identifies a sequence of critical points describing successive stiff-fluid, transient matter-dominated, and stable de-Sitter phases, ensuring a viable thermal history of the universe. The observational and dynamical results are mutually consistent and support the cosmological viability of the proposed models.

paper.title: Dark Matter phase space distribution under a fully relativistic treatment. Eddington inversion according to general relativity
paper.abstract: We develop a fully relativistic extension of Eddington inversion to reconstruct the phase-space distribution function of dark matter from its density profile. Treating dark matter as an effective perfect fluid in a static, spherically symmetric spacetime, we use the Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkoff equations to determine the gravitational background and derive an Abel-type inversion that yields the distribution function in terms of the conserved particle energy measured at infinity. We show that the resulting expression recovers the classical Eddington inversion in the weak-field, nonrelativistic limit. We also investigate the finite-boundary contribution, which can introduce an unphysical divergence, and present a regularization procedure that removes it. We apply our method to a Milky Way model consisting of a generalized Navarro-Frenk-White halo and a Gondolo-Silk dark-matter spike around Sagittarius A$^*$, neglecting baryonic contributions. The relativistic and Newtonian velocity distributions agree at radii far from the Galactic center but begin to differ at distances of order $10^{-5}\,\mathrm{pc}$. Closer to the black hole, the relativistic peak speed can reach approximately twice the Newtonian prediction. Finally, we derive a general expression for dark-matter capture by neutron stars that accommodates arbitrary ambient velocity distributions. Near Sagittarius A$^*$, the relativistic capture factor is nearly an order of magnitude smaller than the Maxwell-Boltzmann prediction, while the Newtonian Eddington result can overestimate it by a factor of approximately two. These results demonstrate the importance of relativistic phase-space reconstruction for dark-matter phenomenology in strong gravitational fields.

paper.title: $El\ Ascua$: An ultra-luminous, radio-loud, Compton-thick AGN at $z\sim 3.8$ hiding in plain sight revealed by MINERVA multi-band MIRI observations
paper.abstract: Heavily dust-obscured active galactic nuclei (AGN) are crucial for understanding supermassive black hole growth. Using multi-band MIRI photometry from the MINERVA survey, we report the discovery in the UDS field of an extremely mid-infrared bright Compton-thick AGN (CT AGN) at $z \sim 3.8$, \textit{el Ascua} (the Ember). The AGN and/or its host galaxy is detected at 870\,$μ$m with ALMA and at 1.4\,GHz with the VLA. With UV-to-radio spectral energy distribution modeling, we estimate that the dusty host galaxy has a stellar mass of $\log\left( M_\star / M_\odot \right)=10.82 \pm 0.57$ and a star formation rate of ${\rm{SFR}} =157 \pm 8 \,M_\odot\,{\rm yr^{-1}}$, and we confirm the presence of a powerful dusty AGN with an intrinsic accretion luminosity of $\log\left( L_{\rm{acc}} /{\rm erg\,s^{-1}} \right)=47.12 \pm 0.58$. CT obscuration is revealed by comparing the upper limit on the X-ray luminosity over $2-10 \,{\rm{keV}}$ with the $6 \,{\rmμ{m}}$ mid-IR AGN luminosity. We additionally find evidence for a radio excess by comparing its total IR-to-radio ratio to those of typical star-forming galaxies and radio-quiet AGN, implying that \textit{el Ascua} could be a rare radio-loud CT AGN. With an extremely high ratio between black hole accretion rate and SFR, the AGN is likely nearing the peak of a deeply obscured phase of black hole growth before AGN feedback blows away the obscuring material. Our work demonstrates the power of MIRI to reveal heavily obscured AGN missing from our supermassive black hole census.

paper.title: Dark Matter and MOND successes and degeneracies in reproducing SPARC rotation curves and weak lensing data
paper.abstract: The observed rotation velocities of spiral galaxies at large scales exceed those predicted by their baryonic components, motivating the need for dark matter (DM) or Modified Newtonian Dynamics (MOND). We fit the rotation curves of 147 late-type galaxies from the SPARC database, using a suite of models including Cold Dark Matter (CDM) models with and without baryonic feedback, Warm DM, Fuzzy DM, and MOND. We also combine SPARC kinematics with weak-lensing data to extend the mean rotation curves to ~1 Mpc. On a galaxy-by-galaxy basis, the inner SPARC rotation curves marginally favour CDM models with baryonic feedback, although accounting for the uncertainties in distances and inclinations increases the degeneracy among DM-based models and MOND. All DM models predict host halo masses larger than abundance-matching expectations, with only the CDM model with baryonic feedback reducing the scatter around the mean luminosity-halo mass relation. MOND is able to reproduce the flatness of the mean galactic rotation curves on scales up to 1 Mpc, providing stellar mass-to-light ratios within observational uncertainties. In contrast, all DM models, without the contribution of mass external to the bound halo, struggle to explain the flat rotation curves. The inclusion of the current weak-lensing data tends to favour MOND over DM models, at least at the largest scales. Future observations from BIG-SPARC, the Square Kilometre Array, and most importantly, upcoming weak-lensing surveys such as EUCLID and Rubin will provide more stringent and independent tests of these competing frameworks

paper.title: SN Ares: A Strongly Lensed Type IIb Supernova at $\mathbf{z=1.276}$ with a Predicted 70-Year Time Delay
paper.abstract: We present the discovery of supernova (SN) Ares, a strongly lensed supernova at $z_{\rm spec}=1.276\pm0.002$ in a massive, triply imaged host galaxy behind the MACS J0308.9+2645 galaxy cluster. JWST/NIRSpec spectroscopy spanning the rest-frame optical to NIR of Ares reveals helium features at $5876\,\mathring{\mathrm{A}}$, $7065\,\mathring{\mathrm{A}}$, and $10830\,\mathring{\mathrm{A}}$, as well as H$α$ and Pa$β$. A comparison to local core-collapse SN spectra and light curves leads to a classification of SN Ares as a Type IIb supernova, the highest-redshift member of its class spectroscopically identified. A comparison to local SN IIb light curves provides a phase estimate for the spectrum of $34_{-9}^{+10}$ rest-frame days post-radioactive peak, providing a unique view into a high-redshift stripped-envelope supernova in its late-photospheric evolution. A lens model of the cluster constructed using recent JWST data indicates that SN Ares is the first image to arrive and will reappear in two future images near the center of the cluster plane in $\gtrsim 70$ years, with predicted magnifications of $\sim5\times$ and $\sim1.5\times$. Planned JWST/NIRSpec Multi-Object Spectroscopy of the cluster will allow for more detailed modeling of the lensed system for tighter constraints on the time delay and magnifications, as well as a template spectrum at the location of SN Ares.

paper.title: The Hosts and Mass Distribution Function of the Most Massive Black Holes: Implications for the nHz Gravitational Wave Background
paper.abstract: We use the core-radius, $r_γ,$ of a galaxy's central core along with a volume-limited sample of brightest cluster galaxies (BCG) to determine the $z=0$ mass distribution function of the most massive super-massive black holes (SMBH). We recover a $M_{BH}-r_γ$ relationship between the SMBH mass, $M_{BH},$ and $r_γ$ of form $M_{BH} \approx1.3\times10^{10}~(r_γ/{\mathrm{kpc}})~M_\odot,$ with $σ= 0.25\pm0.03$ dex scatter in $M_{BH}.$ We derive a core distribution function (CDF), based on HST and DLS images of the BCGs. The CDF falls steeply as $N(r_γ)\sim r_γ^{-3}$ for $r_γ>0.50$ kpc. Only $\sim5\%$ of BCGs have $r_γ>1$ kpc. Combining the CDF and $M_{BH} - r_γ$ relationship yields the BH mass distribution function (MDF). For $M_{BH} \geq 7\times10^{9}~\mathrm{M_\odot}$ (the mean $M_{BH}$ at $r_γ=0.50$ kpc) we derive: $\log\left(\frac{dN(M_{BH})}{d{M_{BH}/10^{10} M_\odot}}~[\rm Mpc^{-3}]\right)=(-3.05\pm0.42)~\log\left(\frac{M_{BH}}{10^{10}M_\odot}\right)~-~5.11\ (+0.41, -0.36)$. Cores with $r_γ\geq 0.50$ kpc are found almost exclusively in BCGs, implying that SMBHs with $M_{BH} \geq7\times10^{9}~\mathrm{M_\odot}$ may also be exclusive to BCGs. Core-radius correlates with $α,$ a parameter that characterizes the growth of BCG envelopes by mergers, suggesting that the most massive SMBHs grew in tandem with their BCG hosts. The BH MDF embodies a significant population of SMBH with $M_{BH} >7\times10^{9} M_\odot.$ When combined with the Liepold & Ma (2024) BH MDF to account for SMBH with $M_{BH} < 7\times10^{9} M_\odot,$ it can comfortably explain the nHz gravitational wave background.
